questions.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Step Functions
questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)}$ for $f(t)=u(t-2)+u(t-5),$ where $u$ is the unit step function.$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise functions $u(t-2)$ and $u(t-5),$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-2) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<2 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 2\end{aligned} \\ u(t-5) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<5 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 5.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
u(t-2)+u(t-5)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<2 \\ 1,\, & 2\le t<5 \\ 2,\, & t\ge 5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, for our Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{5}1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the second integral diverges for $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{2}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{5}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s}]}_{2}^{5}+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{5}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-5s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}(0-{e}^{-5s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{2{e}^{-5s}}{s} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s},\,s>0.
$$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)=u(t-7)$ and $u$ is the unit step function.

$F(s)=L{f(t)}=$
{{field-1}},
valid for $s\,$
{{field-2}}{{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-7)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<7 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 7\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }u(t-7){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{7}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{7}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{7}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{7}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{7}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{7}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-7s}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}(0-{e}^{-7s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-7s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-7s}}{s},\,s>0.
$$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}2,\, & t\le 3 \\ {e}^{t}\, & t>3.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}2,\, & t\le 3 \\ {e}^{t}\, & t>3\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{t-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{(1-s)t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 1.$

For $s>1,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{(1-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{2}{s}{[{e}^{-st}]}_{0}^{3}+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{(1-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-\frac{2{e}^{-3s}}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{(1-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-\frac{2{e}^{-3s}}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{{e}^{(1-s)t}}{1-s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-\frac{2{e}^{-3s}}{s}+\frac{1}{1-s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{(1-s)a}-{e}^{3(1-s)}) \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-\frac{2{e}^{-3s}}{s}+\frac{1}{1-s}\cdot (0-{e}^{3(1-s)}) \\  & =\frac{2}{s}-\frac{2{e}^{-3s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{3(1-s)}}{s-1}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>1.$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t},\, & t\le 3 \\ 1\, & t>3.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t},\, & t\le 3 \\ 1\, & t>3\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{-2t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{-(2+s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{-(2+s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{-(2+s)}{[{e}^{-(2+s)t}]}_{0}^{3}+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-3(2+s)}}{2+s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-3(2+s)}}{2+s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-3(2+s)}}{2+s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-3(2+s)}}{2+s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-3(2+s)}}{2+s}+\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Other Piecewise Continuous Functions
questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t},\, & t\le 4 \\ 2\, & t>4.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t},\, & t\le 4 \\ 2\, & t>4\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{-t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{-(1+s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{-(1+s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{-(1+s)}{[{e}^{-(1+s)t}]}_{0}^{4}+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4(1+s)}}{1+s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{4}^{a}2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4(1+s)}}{1+s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-2{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{4}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4(1+s)}}{1+s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-4s}) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4(1+s)}}{1+s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-4s}) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-4(1+s)}}{1+s}+\frac{2{e}^{-4s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>0.$
